5083               	;
5084               	; 	' HARRY STARTS ON FLOOR 2 AT THE WEST EDGE OF SCREEN 7, and that is as
5085               	; 	' far left as the clock allows. The research says "the second-floor
5086               	; 	' elevator door", which is screen 3, and it cannot be done:
5087               	; 	'
5088               	; 	'   spawn      escape     round
5089               	; 	'   screen 3   119.9 s    100 s   -- impossible
5090               	; 	'   screen 5   108.1 s    100 s   -- impossible
5091               	; 	'   screen 6   102.3 s    100 s   -- impossible
5092               	; 	'   screen 7    96.4 s    100 s   -- 3.6 s of room
5093               	; 	'
5094               	; 	' HE STARTS AT THE LIFT NOW, AND THAT COST HIM A SPEED CHANGE.
5095               	; 	'
5096               	; 	' His escape route ZIGZAGS -- east along floor 2 to its escalator, WEST
5097               	; 	' along floor 3 to that one, then east again along the roof to the door.
5098               	; 	' From the lift on screen 3 that is 5,120 px against the 4,208 he walked
5099               	; 	' from screen 7, so at his old 1.75 px a pass he needed 105 s of a 100 s
5100               	; 	' round: he could never escape at all, and one of the two loss conditions
5101               	; 	' would quietly have stopped existing. This block used to say exactly that
5102               	; 	' and conclude the lift was impossible. It was impossible AT THAT SPEED.
5103               	; 	'
5104               	; 	' AND QUARTER-PIXELS COULD NOT EXPRESS THE ANSWER. A quarter of a pixel
5105               	; 	' per pass is worth about TEN SECONDS of his route, so the two candidate
5106               	; 	' values straddled the buzzer with nothing in between:
5107               	; 	'
5108               	; 	'   2.00 px/pass   escapes at 102.4 s of a 100 s round   never escapes
5109               	; 	'   2.25 px/pass   escapes at  91.0 s                    nine seconds early
5110               	; 	'
5111               	; 	' Worse, 2.25 was not reachable at all: the accumulator below had two
5112               	; 	' drain steps and therefore a hard ceiling of 2 px a pass, so hsp4 = 9
5113               	; 	' silently delivered 2.00 and he fell two thirds of a screen short of his
5114               	; 	' own escape. See the accumulator comment for the full account.
5115               	; 	'
5116               	; 	' Sixteenths with three drains put the step at about 2.5 s instead of 10,
5117               	; 	' and hsp64 = 35 (2.1875 px/pass) lands him at 96.3 s of the 100 --

5396               	;
5397               	; 	' ======================================================================
5398               	; 	' DRAWING THE STORE -- four blits, once per screen crossing
5399               	; 	' ======================================================================
5400               	; 	' This is the whole cost of the flip, and it is paid on a discrete event
5401               	; 	' rather than every frame. RallyX's pan repaints 576 chars every time the
5402               	; 	' camera moves one cell; this repaints 640 about once every two seconds
5403               	; 	' of running.
5404               	; 	' SPRITES OFF BEFORE THE BLIT, NOT AFTER IT. This routine WAITs between
5405               	; 	' bands -- one band a frame, because a burst of VDP writes past a few
5406               	; 	' dozen in one frame is silently dropped -- so painting the new screen
5407               	; 	' takes several frames, and for all of them the OLD screen's actors and
5408               	; 	' obstacles were still sitting on top of it. Following Harry through a
5409               	; 	' seam showed him and every cart from the floor he had just left,
5410               	; 	' standing on a shop that was assembling itself underneath them.
5411               	; 	'
5412               	; 	' They are put back by the normal draw on the same pass, so the crossing
5413               	; 	' reads as a cut rather than as a dissolve with ghosts in it.
5414               	; 	' EACH BAND IS FINISHED BEFORE THE FRAME IT IS DRAWN IN ENDS, and the
5415               	; 	' bands go TOP DOWN. Both halves of that matter.
5416               	; 	'
5417               	; 	' The blit paints the template -- shelves, pillars and all -- and the
5418               	; 	' radios and prizes then take out the fixtures they stand in. Those two
5419               	; 	' used to be four frames apart: all four bands blitted with a WAIT
5420               	; 	' between them, and only afterwards the clearing. So every screen change
5421               	; 	' showed its counters and beams for several frames and then erased them,
5422               	; 	' which reads as the shop flickering rather than as it being drawn.
5423               	; 	'
5424               	; 	' TOP DOWN because a band's beam tops are stamped into the SLAB ROW OF
5425               	; 	' THE BAND ABOVE. Going bottom-up, band 1's blit would paint over the
5426               	; 	' beam tops band 0 had just put there. Going top-down the band above is
5427               	; 	' always already drawn, so everything a band needs -- its own cells and
5428               	; 	' the row it borrows overhead -- is final by the time its WAIT arrives.
5429               	; 	'
5430               	; 	' `3 - dq` rather than `FOR dlv = 3 TO 0 STEP -1`: dlv is an unsigned
5431               	; 	' byte, so counting down past zero wraps to 255 and the loop never ends
5432               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A).
5433               	; draw_screen:
5434               cvb_DRAW_SCREEN

5473               	; 		' clear run at the rows before the beam reaches them. It also still

5579               	;
5580               	; 	' A SUPPORT BEAM HAS TO REACH THE FLOOR IT HOLDS UP, AND THAT FLOOR IS
5581               	; 	' NOT IN ITS OWN BAND. A beam fills its band's four air rows, so its top
5582               	; 	' pixel sits under the slab row of the band ABOVE -- and a slab row is
5583               	; 	' five pixels of bar over three of green (see SLAB), so the beam stopped
5584               	; 	' three pixels short of the bar on every storey. It read as a beam that
5585               	; 	' misses the floor, which is exactly what it was.
5586               	; 	'
5587               	; 	' It cannot be drawn into either template. The beam belongs to the band
5588               	; 	' below and the row belongs to the band above, and the two templates are
5589               	; 	' chosen independently per screen, so no template knows both. So the
5590               	; 	' band blits go down first and the tops are stamped afterwards, from a
5591               	; 	' per-template column table -- the same shape as the escalator's head cap.
5592               	; 	'
5593               	; 	' Bands 0 and 1 only. Band 2's top row is the ROOF DECK, which is grey
5594               	; 	' over grey with no green to bridge, and the roof itself has no band
5595               	; 	' above it at all.
5596               	; 	' BANDS 0 TO 2 -- ALL THREE SHOPPING FLOORS. It used to stop at 1,
5597               	; 	' because band 2's ceiling is the ROOF DECK and the deck had no green
5598               	; 	' under it: a beam there already ran straight into grey and needed
5599               	; 	' nothing. Giving the roof its three green rows (so the lift shaft stops
5600               	; 	' under it, like every other floor) took that away, and the top floor's
5601               	; 	' beams started falling three pixels short.
5602               	; 	'
5603               	; 	' So the roof gets its own version of the stamp. A beam HOLDS THE ROOF
5604               	; 	' UP and must reach it; the shaft merely stops beneath it.

6251               	; 			' the placement table plus a constant -- so the gap between

6260               	; 			' closes on an oncoming hazard at (KWALK64 + its speed)/64

6262               	; 			' eats 82 px of closing distance at the fastest hazard. At
6263               	; 			' 46 or 70 there is NO screen where he can land between the

6380               	; 			' THE BALL IS ON THE GROUND WHEN HE GETS TO IT.
6381               	; 			'
6382               	; 			' The bounce phase used to be `lx AND 31` -- a byte out of
6383               	; 			' the placement table, which is to say arbitrary. Run onto
6384               	; 			' a screen and the first ball might be at the bottom of its
6385               	; 			' arc, where a jump clears it, or at the top, where it has
6386               	; 			' to be ducked, and nothing on the way in told you which.
6387               	; 			' Sometimes you could keep running and jump it; sometimes
6388               	; 			' the same approach at the same speed could not be jumped
6389               	; 			' at all. That is not difficulty, it is a coin toss.
6390               	; 			'
6391               	; 			' So the phase is worked BACKWARDS from the meeting. He
6392               	; 			' closes 4 px a pass and the ball 2, so they meet in
6393               	; 			' (gap / 6) passes; the phase advances one a pass and wraps
6394               	; 			' at 32, so seeding it with the NEGATIVE of that lands it on
6395               	; 			' phase 0 -- the ground -- exactly as they arrive.
6396               	; 			'
6397               	; 			' The gap is the same either way round: he enters at one
6398               	; 			' wall and the ball starts `stag` in from the other, so it
6399               	; 			' is 232 - stag whichever direction the floor runs.
6400               	; 			'
6401               	; 			' It stays forgiving rather than exact. The arc is flat near
6402               	; 			' the bottom, so anything within eight passes either side is
6403               	; 			' still under the jump; and it only holds for an unbroken
6404               	; 			' run, which is the case the player is entitled to read off
6405               	; 			' the screen. Duck, stop or take a hit and everything after
6406               	; 			' is out of step again -- which is the game.

7353               	; 		' what one phase of esc_tick moves the pattern by.
7354               	; 		'

7356               	; 		' is paced by the frame delta, and pacing him that way too made him
7357               	; 		' outrun the steps the moment a pass cost more than one frame: his
7358               	; 		' feet started planted on a tread and ended floating above it.
7359               	; 		' Pacing the ANIMATION by fdv instead is worse -- four phases cannot

7361               	; 		' backwards (see esc_tick). The only arrangement that cannot drift
7362               	; 		' is the one where both are driven by the same fixed step, so the
7363               	; 		' rider is clocked by the pass, like the steps he is standing on.

7678               	; 	' is not a jump, it is flight, and it also let him flip which way he was

8834               	;
8835               	; 	' THE VICTROLA, AS CHARACTERS. It never moves, so a sprite spent a
8836               	; 	' scan-line slot on something that can be painted once when the screen is
8837               	; 	' drawn -- and at one 16x16 sprite it could only ever be one colour and
8838               	; 	' one size. Four cells is twice the area for no sprite at all.
8839               	; 	'
8840               	; 	' It stands ON the slab, so it fills the band's rows 2 and 3; row 4 is
8841               	; 	' the floor bar itself -- and a PRIZE uses those same two rows.
8842               	; 	'
8843               	; 	' THEY CAN SHARE A BAND, AND THE CLAIM THAT USED TO BE HERE WAS WRONG.
8844               	; 	' It said the two never share a screen because "genstore keeps prizes off
8845               	; 	' the screens that carry hazards". That stopped being true the moment
8846               	; 	' hazard placement moved into the per-Krook stor_lvl table, and nothing
8847               	; 	' noticed, because the prize table is not part of the level table and
8848               	; 	' every check was written about one object at a time. Two money bags ended
8849               	; 	' up standing on a radio -- not fighting it, since the two routines poke
8850               	; 	' different cells and the later writer simply wins, so they read as one
8851               	; 	' merged object.
8852               	; 	'
8853               	; 	' WHAT KEEPS THEM APART IS COLUMNS. A radio stands at column 7, 15 or 23
8854               	; 	' (see lrc below); genstore's _off_the_rack nudges a prize clear of all
8855               	; 	' three, and checklevels.py reads that arithmetic back out of THIS file
8856               	; 	' and fails the build on any overlap.
8857               	; 	'
8858               	; 	' rdall = 1 paints all four cells, 0 repaints only the top-right one --
8859               	; 	' the pulse. Same address arithmetic either way, so the two cannot drift.
8860               	; 	' A BEAM TOP HANGS OUT OF THE FLOOR ABOVE, and the beam it belongs to has
8861               	; 	' just been taken away. `beam_tops` stamps SLABP -- the floor bar with the
8862               	; 	' support carried up through its lower three pixel rows -- into the slab
8863               	; 	' row above every pillar, and it runs BEFORE the radios and prizes are
8864               	; 	' placed. Clearing a pillar's own cells therefore left three grey pixels
8865               	; 	' dangling from the ceiling with nothing under them.
8866               	; 	'
8867               	; 	' TESTED, NOT ASSUMED: only SLABP is put back to SLAB. The row above the
8868               	; 	' top shopping floor is the ROOF DECK, a different character altogether,
8869               	; 	' and writing a floor bar over it would punch a hole in the roof.
8870               	; 	' A SHELF RUN IS FIVE CELLS WIDE and a radio covers two, so one standing
8871               	; 	' on a counter punched a hole through its middle and left the ends either
8872               	; 	' side -- the same incoherence the dangling pillar had, and worse, because
8873               	; 	' a counter reads as one object. The whole unit goes: walk outward along
8874               	; 	' the band's row 2 while the cell is still a shelf top, clearing it and
8875               	; 	' its bottom half together.
8876               	; 	'
8877               	; 	' Bounded at eight steps. The runs are five, so eight is slack rather
8878               	; 	' than a guess -- and an unbounded walk would run off the end of the row
8879               	; 	' if the name table ever held something unexpected.
8880               	; 	#if NES
8881               	; 	' WHAT THE TEMPLATE PUT IN THIS CELL, for a target that cannot read its
8882               	; 	' own video memory back. #nta is the offset INSIDE the band (0-159) and
8883               	; 	' nbl is the band; the answer is the byte SCREEN blitted there.
8884               	; 	'
8885               	; 	' This is the same arithmetic the blit itself does in draw_band --
8886               	; 	' template id out of stor_ix for (band, screen), times 160, plus the
8887               	; 	' offset -- so the two cannot disagree about what is on screen. It is
8888               	; 	' reading what the cell MEANS, not guessing from where the cell is: a
8889               	; 	' coordinate is a fact about this layout, the character is a fact about
8890               	; 	' the world, and only the second is safe to erase on.
8891               	; 	' SIXTEEN PATTERNS INTO THE BORROWED SLOTS, ONE VBLANK EACH.
8892               	; 	'
8893               	; 	' This is what esc_stand and esc_run cost on this machine. Four sprites is
8894               	; 	' 16 patterns and **a tile here is SIXTEEN bytes** -- two bitplanes -- so
8895               	; 	' the swap is 256 bytes. Three ways to spend that, and only one works:
8896               	; 	'
8897               	; 	'   nes_def         rendering off, ~2 frames of DARK SCREEN every mount.
8898               	; 	'                   This is the flash that was reported for three sessions.
8899               	; 	'   resident art    no upload at all -- but it needs 16 free patterns per
8900               	; 	'                   facing and there are only twelve free in the whole
8901               	; 	'                   table. Tried, and it overwrote Harry's left-facing legs.
8902               	; 	'   queued, chunked <- this. 64 bytes a vblank, four vblanks, picture up
8903               	; 	'                   the whole time.
8904               	; 	'
8905               	; 	' FOUR CHUNKS BECAUSE ONE WILL NOT FIT. The NMI's copy loop runs to the end
8906               	; 	' of its descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and the PPUADDR/PPUSCROLL
8907               	; 	' restore that follows it re-points the PPU mid-frame if it runs late --
8908               	; 	' which is the whole picture jumping for a frame. About 1679 cycles are
8909               	; 	' available after OAM DMA and a copy costs 50 + 14 a byte, so 64 bytes
8910               	; 	' (946) is comfortable and 256 (3634) is not. The WAITs are load-bearing:
8911               	; 	' PPUBUF accumulates for a whole pass, so without them all four descriptors
8912               	; 	' would flush in one vblank and cost exactly what the single call did.
8913               	; 	' checkvblank.py sums the descriptors BETWEEN WAITs for this reason.
8914               	; 	'
8915               	; 	' The cost is four frames at a mount or a dismount, once each, against two
8916               	; 	' frames of black. The caller sets #nsrc; nes_chrinit copies nchr, ncnt,
8917               	; 	' #ncol and nink into zero page rather than consuming the variables, so
8918               	; 	' they only need setting once.
8919               	; 	'
8920               	; 	' THE INTERMEDIATE STATE IS VISIBLE and that is accepted: for a frame or
8921               	; 	' two Harry is part standing and part running. He is stepping onto a
8922               	; 	' staircase at the time, which is exactly when a limb changing shape reads
8923               	; 	' as him changing pose.
8924               	; nes_swp16:
8925               	; 	' HARRY COMES OFF THE SCREEN FIRST, because this takes four frames.
8926               	; 	'
8927               	; 	' The swap is 256 bytes and a vblank carries about a hundred, so it goes as
8928               	; 	' four queued chunks with a WAIT between them (see below). The game loop is
8929               	; 	' stopped for those frames but the PPU is not, so whatever is half-written
8930               	; 	' is on screen: for a frame or two Harry was part standing and part
8931               	; 	' running -- reported as a glitch when he steps off a flight, and it is
8932               	; 	' one. All four of his sprites differ between the two poses, so there is no
8933               	; 	' ordering of the chunks that stays coherent.
8934               	; 	'
8935               	; 	' He is hidden instead. Four frames of absence at the exact moment he steps
8936               	; 	' on or off a staircase reads as nothing at all, where a figure assembled
8937               	; 	' out of two poses reads as a fault. draw_actors puts him back on its next
8938               	; 	' pass -- no flag to clear, because it writes all four slots every time.
8939               	; 	'
8940               	; 	' AND THE OAM MIRRORS WITH HIM. nes_oam2 copies slots 0-27 into 28-55 to
8941               	; 	' make each 16x16 actor two NES sprites, and it only runs at the end of
8942               	; 	' draw_actors -- which is not running during these WAITs. Without the call
8943               	; 	' below his left half would vanish and his RIGHT half would stay, which is
8944               	; 	' a worse artefact than the one being fixed.
8945               	; 	SPRITE 4,SPRHID,0,0,0
8946               	; 	SPRITE 5,SPRHID,0,0,0
8947               	; 	SPRITE 6,SPRHID,0,0,0
8948               	; 	SPRITE 7,SPRHID,0,0,0
8949               	; 	ASM JSR nes_oam2
8950               	; 	ASM JSR nes_suitcases
8951               	; 	nchr = P_HSTB
8952               	; 	ntab = 0
8953               	; 	#ncol = 0
8954               	; 	nink = 1
8955               	; 	ncnt = 4
8956               	; 	WAIT
8957               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
8958               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32		' four patterns of source art, 8 bytes each
8959               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
8960               	; 	WAIT
8961               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
8962               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32

8964               	; 	WAIT

8966               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32

8973               	; 	' Setup only, just like nes_def; never called from the play loop.
8974               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrraw
8975               	; 	RETURN
8976               	;
8977               	; nes_def:
8978               	; 	' WHAT DEFINE WOULD HAVE DONE. CVBasic implements no DEFINE at all for the
8979               	; 	' NES, on the reading that patterns live in cartridge CHR ROM -- but an
8980               	; 	' iNES header with a CHR-bank count of ZERO asks for 8 KB of CHR-RAM
8981               	; 	' instead, and that is the header CVBasic emits whenever the program uses
8982               	; 	' no BITMAP/CHRROM statement. So the pattern table here is ordinary VRAM
8983               	; 	' and this is the write. assets/nes_chr.asm carries the routine and the
8984               	; 	' reasoning; the caller sets #nsrc, nchr, ncnt and ntab.
8985               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrup
8986               	; 	RETURN
8987               	;
8988               	; 	' AND THE SAME THING WITHOUT LOSING A FRAME. nes_def turns rendering off
8989               	; 	' and waits for a vblank the NMI therefore never services, so the game's
8990               	; 	' own WAIT then waits for the one after -- about two frames a call. That
8991               	; 	' is free at setup and ruinous anywhere that runs repeatedly. It builds
8992               	; 	' the same bytes into `nesb` and hands the NMI a single copy descriptor
8993               	; 	' instead. See assets/nes_chr.asm.
8994               	; 	'
8995               	; 	' THE NAME IS HISTORICAL: it was written for esc_tick, which redefines six
8996               	; 	' characters EVERY PASS on the two escalator screens and ran visibly slow
8997               	; 	' on nes_def. Nothing about it is escalator-specific -- it takes the same
8998               	; 	' inputs as nes_def plus #nesb, and the title's marquee uses it too, where
8999               	; 	' nes_def was switching the picture off twice a step and reading as a
9000               	; 	' flashing title screen.
9001               	; 	'
9002               	; 	' #nesb must point at a buffer of at least ncnt*16 bytes and is set once
9003               	; 	' in init_tables, which runs before boot: and therefore before the title.
9004               	; nes_escd:

9812               	; 	' THE BOUNCE PHASE, ON THE SAME CLOCK AS THE JUMP AND AT ITS OLD PERIOD.

9815               	; 	' the bounce advanced once per PASS -- so whether a jump cleared a ball
9816               	; 	' depended on how busy the screen was, and the frame-by-frame property
9817               	; 	' checkball.py proves was exact only at fdv = 1.
9818               	; 	'
9819               	; 	' Stepping the phase by fdv directly would fix the clock and wreck the
9820               	; 	' game: a 32-phase arc would drop from about 1.35 s to 0.55 s, balls
9821               	; 	' bouncing 2.4x faster everywhere. So it gets a fraction of its own --
9822               	; 	' 25/64 of a phase per frame is 23.4 phases a second, against the 23.8 it
9823               	; 	' runs at today. Same bounce, now the same clock as the thing that has to
9824               	; 	' clear it.

10089               	;
10090               	; 	' ONE STEP OF A FRACTIONAL SPEED, FOR WHOEVER IS MOVING.
10091               	; 	'
10092               	; 	' `pacc` in and out, `psp64` in (sixty-fourths of a pixel per FRAME),
10093               	; 	' `pspd` out (whole pixels this pass). CVBasic has no locals, so the caller
10094               	; 	' stages its own accumulator in and takes it back out; that costs four
10095               	; 	' statements against the fourteen this used to be, written out per actor.
10096               	; 	'
10097               	; 	' Harry had the only copy. Kelly, the hazards and the bounce phase all need
10098               	; 	' the same thing -- everything the round clock judges has to advance by
10099               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAMES, or the loop rate becomes a difficulty dial and where the
10100               	; 	' player stands decides the outcome (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10101               	; 	'
10102               	; 	' Three drains support up to 192/64 units per frame. The remainder
10103               	; 	' is below 64, so the byte addition cannot exceed 255. Planes use
10104               	; 	' two-pixel units and double the result outside this shared routine.
10105               	; 	' Other actors retain pixel units and their existing movement rates.
10106               	; 	'
10107               	; 	' FIVE FRAMES, AND THREE WAS TOO FEW. At 2 px a frame five frames is 10 px,
10108               	; 	' and to skip a position window an actor must start outside it on one side
10109               	; 	' and land outside on the other, which needs 12. Three was the original bug
10110               	; 	' in miniature: the lift screen runs at almost exactly 20 passes a second,
10111               	; 	' which IS fdv = 3, so every hitch there lost a frame. The clamp exists for
10112               	; 	' a genuine stall and at five it only fires for one.
10113               	; pace_step:
10114               cvb_PACE_STEP

10617               	;
10618               	; 	' THE SIXTEENTH-PIXEL ACCUMULATOR. hx is one unsigned byte per screen
10619               	; 	' (2), so there is nowhere to keep a fraction -- the fraction lives here
10620               	; 	' and is spent as whole pixels. THREE IFs, not a loop and not a divide:
10621               	; 	' `%` and `/` both compile to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and this
10622               	; 	' runs every pass.
10623               	; 	'
10624               	; 	' THE NUMBER OF DRAINS IS A CEILING ON THE SPEED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE
10625               	; 	' POINT OF THIS COMMENT. Each IF can spend one whole pixel, so N drains
10626               	; 	' cap hspd at N px per pass NO MATTER WHAT hsp64 SAYS. The invariant is:
10627               	; 	'
10628               	; 	'     hacc is under 16 on entry, and hsp64 is at most 48,
10629               	; 	'     so hacc is under 64 here and three drains always suffice.
10630               	; 	'
10631               	; 	' KEEP hsp64 <= 48. This was quarter-pixels with TWO drains and the same
10632               	; 	' invariant written the same way -- "hsp4 is at most 8, so it can never
10633               	; 	' need a third" -- and it was correct until somebody set hsp4 = 9 without
10634               	; 	' re-reading it. The crook then ran at a flat 2.0 px/pass while every
10635               	; 	' comment, the design table and assets/checkchase.py all said 2.25, and
10636               	; 	' the surplus quarter leaked into hacc and wrapped the byte every 256
10637               	; 	' passes. Nothing failed; he simply arrived two thirds of a screen short
10638               	; 	' of his own escape. checkchase.py now counts these IFs and refuses a
10639               	; 	' speed the drains cannot deliver.
10640               	; 	'
10641               	; 	' 7, NOT 6, AND THE REASON IS MEASURED. Tracked off the reference video
10642               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 4a), the 2600's Kelly covers 0.40 screen widths a second and
10643               	; 	' its Harry 0.193 -- a ratio of 2.07. At hsp4 = 6 ours was 2.67, and the
10644               	; 	' crook visibly strolled. 7 brings it to 2.29. 8 would match the original
10645               	; 	' exactly and cannot be used: Kelly's route here is 1.95x Harry's, so a
10646               	; 	' speed ratio of 2.0 leaves the on-foot chase 0.2 s of slack, which is no
10647               	; 	' chase at all. checkchase.py holds the line.
10648               	; 	' STILL RUNNING FROM THE STAIRS -- and this has to come BEFORE the move,

10749               	; 	' HE WALKS BY REAL TIME, NOT BY LOOP PASS -- one accumulate-and-drain per
10750               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAME rather than per pass. Everything that moves here used to be
10751               	; 	' per pass while the CLOCK is paced by the frame delta, so a busy screen
10752               	; 	' slowed Harry in real seconds and the clock did not slow with him: the
10753               	; 	' same uninterrupted escape finished with nine timer units in hand from a
10754               	; 	' light screen and none at all from the lift screen, decided by where the
10755               	; 	' player happened to be standing. Now he covers the same ground per second
10756               	; 	' wherever anybody is (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10757               	; 	'
10758               	; 	' A LOOP, NOT A MULTIPLY. `*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, and reading a
10759               	; 	' 16-bit variable straight after one returns the product's HIGH word
10760               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). fdv is 1..3 here, so this is at most three adds.
10761               	; 	'
10762               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS, AND ONLY TWO DRAINS -- both fall out of accumulating per
10763               	; 	' FRAME instead of per pass. He covers under a pixel a frame, so two drains
10764               	; 	' are ample where the per-pass version needed three; and the finer unit is
10765               	; 	' what makes the speed tunable at all. In sixteenths one step was about six
10766               	; 	' SECONDS of his route, so nothing landed near the buzzer; in sixty-fourths
10767               	; 	' it is about one and a half. Keep hsp64 <= 128: hacc is under 64 on entry,
10768               	; 	' so 64 + 128 stays inside a byte and two drains always suffice.
10769               	; 	'
10770               	; 	' AND THE STEP IS CLAMPED TO THREE FRAMES' WORTH, WHICH IS NOT A DETAIL.
10771               	; 	' Two tests sample his position once a pass and neither interpolates:
10772               	; 	'
10773               	; 	'   ARRIVAL   `hdx < 6` around the escalator or the roof door -- an ELEVEN
10774               	; 	'             pixel window. A step over 10 px can jump clean across it and
10775               	; 	'             he never arrives at all.
10776               	; 	'   THE CATCH `hdd < CATCHR` is 12, a 23-wide band, and Kelly closes 4 of
10777               	; 	'             it himself -- so Harry over ~18 px could pass through the Kop
10778               	; 	'             between two passes without either sample being inside it.
10779               	; 	'
10780               	; 	' The clamp and the drains live in pace_step now, with the reasoning; the
10781               	; 	' numbers above are what sized them. Measured: TIME 02 on the lift screen
10782               	; 	' against TIME 04 on a light one when the clamp was 3, and 00 against 09
10783               	; 	' before any of this.
10784               	; 	'
10785               	; 	' The ESCALATOR RIDE is deliberately untouched: it returns above this,
10786               	; 	' clocked one step per pass to stay locked to the moving staircase. A rider
10787               	; 	' advanced by the frame delta either drifts off the treads or makes the
10788               	; 	' steps run backwards (CLAUDE.md 3A, DESIGN.md 0f). It is about 3% of his
10789               	; 	' journey.
10790               	; 	'
10791               	; 	' `hanim` still advances by hspd and is still an ODOMETER -- pixels
10792               	; 	' travelled, not time -- so the run cycle stays locked to the ground at any
10793               	; 	' rate. A 9 px step moves it exactly one pose of its 8 px beat.
10794               	; 	pacc = hacc

11254               	;
11255               	; 	' ======================================================================
11256               	; 	' COLLISIONS -- pure arithmetic against RAM, no VDP reads
11257               	; 	' ======================================================================
11258               	; 	' Kelly's box is [kfh, kfh + kh) above the slab; an obstacle's is
11259               	; 	' [ohb, oht). The ball's inset hitbox is what makes 8..10 avoidable both
11260               	; 	' ways -- without it there is a height at which the ball can be neither
11261               	; 	' jumped nor ducked, and an unavoidable hazard is not difficulty.
11262               	; 	' ONE HIT PER CONTACT, WITH A REFRACTORY PERIOD.
11263               	; 	'
11264               	; 	' The overlap test is true on every frame the player is touching
11265               	; 	' something, so with no latch at all one clumsy cart charges nine seconds
11266               	; 	' several times over -- and what the player sees is the clock jumping by
11267               	; 	' 27, from which the only available conclusion is that the penalty is
11268               	; 	' broken.
11269               	; 	'
11270               	; 	' A latch that clears on the first non-overlapping frame is still not
11271               	; 	' enough, and the case that breaks it is the BOUNCING BALL: it rises off
11272               	; 	' the player between bounces, which is a genuine loss of contact, so a
11273               	; 	' player standing still under one is taxed on every single bounce while
11274               	; 	' being given no opportunity to do anything about it. Technically two
11275               	; 	' collisions; in play, one situation.
11276               	; 	'
11277               	; 	' So obht() is a countdown, not a flag. A hit sets it to HITREF; it ticks
11278               	; 	' down only while the player is CLEAR, and the same obstacle cannot charge
11279               	; 	' again until it reaches zero. Contact holds the count up, so parking
11280               	; 	' inside something never earns a second penalty either.
11281               	; coll_obst:
11282               cvb_COLL_OBST

11722               	; 	' THE FLOOR CLEARS WHEN YOU ARE HIT, and stays clear until you re-enter
11723               	; 	' the screen. Nine seconds is a heavy penalty on a fifty-unit clock, and
11724               	; 	' taking it while still standing among the things that charged it -- with
11725               	; 	' a second hazard 48 px behind the first -- is how one mistake becomes
11726               	; 	' three. Clearing the row makes the penalty a single event you can walk
11727               	; 	' away from.
11728               	; 	'
11729               	; 	' BOTH SLOTS, WHATEVER IS IN THEM. Radios used to be exempt: they are
11730               	; 	' CHARACTERS stamped into the name table rather than sprites, so zeroing
11731               	; 	' the kind would have stopped them colliding while leaving them plainly
11732               	; 	' visible on the shelf, and a fixture that is still there has to still be
11733               	; 	' there. That was a reason to UNDRAW them, not a reason to keep them --
11734               	; 	' and it left the one hazard that cannot leave on its own as the only one
11735               	; 	' the mercy did not cover. haz_off now takes the characters with it.
11736               	; 	'
11737               	; 	' NOTHING RESTORES IT HERE. load_band repopulates the band from the
11738               	; 	' template, and it runs only on a seam crossing or a round start, so
11739               	; 	' "until the screen is re-entered" costs no state and no timer: leave and
11740               	; 	' come back and the hazards are simply placed again.
11741               	; 	'
11742               	; 	' THE CALL ITSELF IS IN THE MAIN LOOP, at the end of the freeze -- see
11743               	; 	' the hfz block there for why.

11745               	; 	' which dropped him straight down out of mid-air onto whatever he happened
11746               	; 	' to be over -- and since the arc is ballistic and ignores the stick once
11747               	; 	' he is airborne (0l), that read as the game taking the controls away

11911               	; 	' AND THEY HAVE TO BE AT THE SAME HEIGHT, NOT MERELY ON THE SAME FLOOR.
11912               	; 	'
11913               	; 	' `hlv` does not change until a ride ENDS -- a crook stepping onto a
11914               	; 	' flight keeps the floor he left until he arrives at the next one. So
11915               	; 	' while he was most of a storey up or down the stairs he still counted as
11916               	; 	' standing on the floor he started from, and a Kop who ran over the head
11917               	; 	' of the flight arrested him through the floor. Reported from play:
11918               	; 	' "I run over top of him, even though we do not touch".
11919               	; 	'
11920               	; 	' It is the same shape of bug as the catch that fired at MAXIMUM
11921               	; 	' separation: a test that is right about one axis and silent about the
11922               	; 	' other, where the silent one happens to be true nearly all the time.
11923               	; 	'
11924               	; 	' UNSIGNED-SAFE. Riding up is above the shared floor and riding down is
11925               	; 	' below it, which is a signed quantity, and CVBasic's variables are not.
11926               	; 	' So both are collected as POSITIVE heights on opposite sides -- Kelly's
11927               	; 	' climb plus Harry's descent on one side, Harry's climb on the other --
11928               	; 	' and the difference is taken between two numbers that cannot go
11929               	; 	' negative. Two riders passing on the same flight measure the sum of
11930               	; 	' their heights, which is exactly the distance between them.

12496               	; 	' HIS ARMS SWING, on the same bit of the animation counter that picks the
12497               	; 	' legs -- so the arm that is forward is the one opposite the leading leg,
12498               	; 	' which is what running looks like.

12500               	; 	'
12501               	; 	' Bit 8 is one BEAT, and the legs take four of them (bits 8 and 16). So an
12502               	; 	' arm swing keyed to bit 8 completed twice for every one pass of the legs:
12503               	; 	' the top half of him flapping at double the speed of the bottom half.
12504               	; 	' That is the jig. It is not a drawing problem and no amount of redrawing
12505               	; 	' the legs would have touched it.
12506               	; 	'
12507               	; 	' On bit 16 the arms hold through beats 1-2 and swap for 3-4, which is
12508               	; 	' also the right PHASE: beat 1 leads with one leg and beat 3 with the
12509               	; 	' other, so the arm opposite the leading leg is forward in each -- which
12510               	; 	' is what running looks like.
12511               	; 	' THE TORSO RUNS ON THE SAME TWO BITS AS THE LEGS. With four drawn poses
12512               	; 	' the shoulders and arms swing WITH the stride; the old two-frame body had
12513               	; 	' a clock of its own, which is what read as a flap rather than a run.

13110               	; 	' ======================================================================
13111               	; 	' THE SCANNER
13112               	; 	' ======================================================================
13113               	; 	' Rows 21-23, 16 chars wide, centred: 48 characters whose PATTERNS are
13114               	; 	' poked directly, so a moving dot costs two writes and no name-table
13115               	; 	' traffic. With the flip (DESIGN.md 2a) this is how you know where Harry
13116               	; 	' is at all -- he can be one pixel off-screen and completely invisible.
13117               	; 	'
13118               	; 	' Rows 21-23 all sit in the THIRD screen third, so every scanner pattern
13119               	; 	' is at base 4096 and no third-selection arithmetic is needed.
13120               	; 	'
13121               	; 	' BOTH DOTS ARE WHITE and Kelly's BLINKS. The manual wants Kelly black
13122               	; 	' and Harry white, but this is the TMS9918's two-colours-per-8x1-cell
13123               	; 	' mode: a black dot and a white dot on the same pixel row of the same
13124               	; 	' character cannot both exist. Blinking distinguishes them with one
13125               	; 	' colour, which is what RallyX does with its player dot.
13126               	; 	' THE STEPS MOVE, AND EVERY ESCALATOR ON SCREEN MOVES WITH THEM. A flight
13127               	; 	' is twelve characters -- six per direction, sliced out of a rendered
13128               	; 	' 64x40 bitmap by genart.py -- so rewriting those twelve PATTERNS animates
13129               	; 	' the lot: 96 bytes, no name-table traffic, and the same cost whether one
13130               	; 	' flight is visible or ten. The phases slide the cells ALONG the slope, so
13131               	; 	' the steps travel up the flight rather than drifting sideways.
13132               	; esc_tick:
13133               cvb_ESC_TICK
13134               	; 	' ONLY SCREENS 0 AND 7 CARRY A FLIGHT, so six screens in eight skip this
13135               	; 	' entirely -- which is what makes rewriting the cells every frame
13136               	; 	' affordable. Nested, not `klsc > 0 AND klsc < 7`: the 9900 backend
13137               	; 	' miscompiles a compare-AND-compare (CLAUDE.md 3A).
13138               	; 	IF klsc > 0 THEN

13157               	; 	' ONE PHASE PER PASS, AND NEVER MORE. There are four phases covering an
13158               	; 	' 8 px period, so advancing by the frame delta ALIASES: at fdv 2 the
13159               	; 	' pattern flips between two positions half a period apart and the
13160               	; 	' direction stops being readable, and at fdv 3 the sequence runs 0,3,2,1
13161               	; 	' -- the staircase visibly runs BACKWARDS, carrying its steps down while
13162               	; 	' the rider goes up. That is the wagon-wheel effect, and no amount of
13163               	; 	' phase arithmetic fixes it: a 4-phase cycle can only be stepped by 1.
13164               	; 	'
13165               	; 	' So the ANIMATION is the clock here, and the rider is paced from it --
13166               	; 	' see move_kelly, which advances him by the same fixed 2-and-1 per pass
13167               	; 	' rather than by fdv. Locking the two together is the only way they
13168               	; 	' cannot drift, and it is what "the player moves at the rate the steps
13169               	; 	' carry him" actually means. The cost is that a ride takes 36 passes
13170               	; 	' rather than 36 frames, so it slows down when the loop does -- which is
13171               	; 	' the honest behaviour for a machine that is carrying you.
13172               	; 	escp = escp + 1

     E598 20AD     
13184               cv829
13185               	; 	#if NES
13186               	; 	' A VBLANK OF ITS OWN, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE-SCREEN FLASH.
13187               	; 	'
13188               	; 	' PPUBUF is not flushed when it is written -- it ACCUMULATES for the whole
13189               	; 	' pass and the NMI empties it in one go, so every VPOKE the radar makes,
13190               	; 	' every HUD digit and this upload all land in the SAME vblank. And the
13191               	; 	' handler's copy loop does not stop when vblank ends: it runs to the end of
13192               	; 	' the descriptor and then writes PPUADDR and both PPUSCROLLs, which
13193               	; 	' mid-frame re-points the PPU's own render address. The rest of that frame
13194               	; 	' is drawn from the wrong place. On screen that is not a dropped tile, it
13195               	; 	' is the ENTIRE PICTURE jumping for a frame -- which is what has been
13196               	; 	' reported, repeatedly, as the screen flashing on an escalator.
13197               	; 	'
13198               	; 	' The arithmetic says it cannot be anything else. NTSC vblank is about
13199               	; 	' 2273 CPU cycles; NMI entry, the flicker test and OAM DMA spend ~560 of
13200               	; 	' them before a single byte is copied. A copy descriptor costs ~50 cycles
13201               	; 	' plus 14 a byte, so these six characters -- 96 bytes, because a tile is
13202               	; 	' SIXTEEN bytes in two bitplanes, not eight -- are ~1400 on their own.
13203               	; 	' That leaves about 270 cycles, or SIX single-byte pokes, for everything
13204               	; 	' else the pass queued. The radar alone beats that whenever a dot moves.
13205               	; 	'
13206               	; 	' Nothing smaller fixes it, because the overrun is per FRAME, not per
13207               	; 	' second: slowing the animation down just makes the bad frames rarer.
13208               	; 	' Splitting the six characters across two frames tears the staircase, and
13209               	; 	' only three of the six have a constant second bitplane, so dropping a
13210               	; 	' plane does not buy a frame's worth either. What DOES work is giving the
13211               	; 	' upload a vblank with nothing else in it: this WAIT flushes the pass's
13212               	; 	' radar and HUD writes, and the descriptor queued below is then almost all
13213               	; 	' the next vblank has to carry -- ~1960 cycles of 2273, inside the window
13214               	; 	' with room to spare.
13215               	; 	'
13216               	; 	' IT COSTS ONE FRAME A PASS, on the two screens that carry a flight and
13217               	; 	' nowhere else -- esc_tick has already returned on the other six. The
13218               	; 	' rider is paced from the animation rather than from the frame delta (see
13219               	; 	' below), so a slower pass slows the ride too and the two cannot drift.
13220               	; 	WAIT
13221               	; 	#endif
13222               	; 	' ONLY THE CELLS THAT MOVE, AND ONLY THIS SCREEN'S. genart.py measures
13223               	; 	' which cells move -- the step cells and the COMPOSITE copies of them
13224               	; 	' that cross a floor -- and groups them WEST then EAST, because only one
13225               	; 	' direction is ever on screen: screen 0 carries a west flight and screen
13226               	; 	' 7 an east one.
13227               	; 	'
13228               	; 	' THIS IS THE ONLY PER-PASS WORK UNIQUE TO THESE TWO SCREENS, and it is
13229               	; 	' `define_char`, which in bitmap mode is LDIRVM3 -- the TRIPLE copy, once
13230               	; 	' per screen third. It therefore costs three times what the character
13231               	; 	' count suggests, which is why these screens run slower than the rest.

13570               	;
13571               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------- the scanner's furniture
13572               	; 	' Without this the scanner is two dots in a void: you can see THAT Harry is
13573               	; 	' somewhere, but not what he is near, which is the one thing you actually
13574               	; 	' need when he is off-screen. Floor lines say which level, the slashes say
13575               	; 	' where that floor's escalator is, and the bar says where the elevator is --
13576               	; 	' exactly the three things the manual lists.
13577               	; 	'
13578               	; 	' FURNITURE AND DOTS ARE SEGREGATED BY PIXEL ROW ON PURPOSE, and a level
13579               	; 	' band is now FOUR rows, one per colour, because a pixel row carries
13580               	; 	' exactly one colour here:
13581               	; 	'
13582               	; 	'   +0  GREY    escalator head, and the elevator car
13583               	; 	'   +1  GREY    the air of that floor
13584               	; 	'   +2  GREY
13585               	; 	'   +3  YELLOW  the floor line -- and NOTHING else goes here
13586               	; 	'
13587               	; 	' THE FIRST THREE ROWS ARE THE FLOOR'S AIR AND EVERYTHING LIVES IN THEM:
13588               	; 	' the escalator's three-step diagonal, the lift car, and both actors, all
13589               	; 	' three pixels tall. They are grey in the table, and the Kop and the
13590               	; 	' crook recolour their own CHARACTER as they move (scan_mark) -- which is
13591               	; 	' what lets both of them fill the band instead of getting a pixel row
13592               	; 	' each. Eight pixels of this canvas is half a screen of the store, so
13593               	; 	' they are almost never in one character; when they are, they merge.
13594               	; 	'
13595               	; 	' Shrinking from six rows bought eight empty pixel rows, four above the
13596               	; 	' instrument and four below, so it no longer butts against the shop floor
13597               	; 	' above it or the bottom of the screen.
13598               	; 	'
13599               	; 	' The dots are erased by ANDing their bits out, so anything sharing a row
13600               	; 	' with one is rubbed away wherever an actor has passed -- which is why
13601               	; 	' scan_escs and scan_elev redraw every tick rather than once.
13602               	; scan_furn:
13603               cvb_SCAN_FURN
13604               	; 	FOR fl = 0 TO 3
13605 E79A 04C0  14 	clr r0
13606 E79C D800  38 	movb r0,@cvb_FL
     E79E 21C6

13871               	; 	'
13872               	; 	' It was six everywhere once. It shrank to four to buy eight empty pixel
13873               	; 	' rows -- four above the instrument and four below -- so the scanner did
13874               	; 	' not butt against the shop floor above it and the bottom of the screen.
13875               	; 	'

13877               	; 	' thirty rows to the TI's twenty-four, so the strip runs past the canvas to
13878               	; 	' the bottom edge and the grey either side of the instrument is real cells
13879               	; 	' rather than blank rows inside it. That gives the band its two rows back,
13880               	; 	' and the instrument goes from 16 pixels tall to 24 -- half again, which is
13881               	; 	' what "not quite so vertically thin" asks for.

14043               	;
14044               	; 	' Blank the canvas by WRITING zeros rather than copying 384 of them out
14045               	; 	' of ROM. This runs twice a game -- at setup and on a new Krook -- so a
14046               	; 	' loop costs nothing anybody can perceive, and it hands the fixed area
14047               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that
14048               	; 	' actually binds. Paced in bursts: a few hundred VDP writes in a single
14049               	; 	' frame are silently dropped (CLAUDE.md 3A).
14050               	; scan_wipe:
14051               cvb_SCAN_WIPE
14052               	; 	' THIS ADDRESS IS A CHARACTER CODE IN DISGUISE, AND IT WENT STALE.
14053               	; 	' 4096 is the pattern table's BOTTOM THIRD -- rows 16-23, which is
14054               	; 	' band 0 and the radar together -- and the canvas characters begin at
14055               	; 	' genart's SCAN_FIRST, so the base is 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8. It was
14056               	; 	' written out by hand as 4096 + 160*8 when SCAN_FIRST was 160; art
14057               	; 	' added later moved SCAN_FIRST to 208 and nothing moved this with it,
14058               	; 	' so the wipe zeroed the 48 characters BELOW the canvas and never
14059               	; 	' touched the canvas at all.
14060               	; 	'
14061               	; 	' Two of those forty-eight are STRUCTURE. ENDWALL is the building's
14062               	; 	' outside wall and SLABP is a pillar's cap. Blanking a pattern in ONE
14063               	; 	' THIRD leaves a character that draws correctly everywhere else and
14064               	; 	' falls back to its own background colour here -- so the GROUND FLOOR's
14065               	; 	' outside wall turned into plain green while the identical wall one
14066               	; 	' storey up was perfect, and the ground floor's pillars lost the brick
14067               	; 	' carried up through the bar above them. ENDWALL appears only on
14068               	; 	' screens 0 and 7, which is exactly why it was reported as happening
14069               	; 	' only on the escalator screens, mirrored side to side.
14070               	; 	'
14071               	; 	' The name table was correct the whole time. Probing it said so, four
14072               	; 	' times. It was the GLYPH that was empty, in one third only -- which a
14073               	; 	' probe that copies the character somewhere else to look at it cannot
14074               	; 	' see, because the copy renders from a different third's pattern.
14075               	; 	'
14076               	; 	' renumber.py rewrites this line from genart.SCAN_FIRST, and
14077               	; 	' checkstruct.py fails the build if the two disagree.

14687               	;
14688               	; #if NES
14689               	; 	' ----------------------------------------------------------------------
14690               	; 	' Attributes select a palette per 16x16 quadrant. gennescolor.py derives
14691               	; 	' eight screen tables; draw_screen stages one in nesb, masks fixtures,
14692               	; 	' then uploads all 64 bytes through nes_attrs_put within one vblank.
14693               	; 	' A MESSAGE BOX GOES GOLD ON DARK BLUE, and the caller says which four
14694               	; 	' bytes in #nav.
14695               	; 	'
14696               	; 	' The text's paper is index 1 and its ink index 3 (see the font upload);
14697               	; 	' over the store those are P0's green and gold -- the same green the box is
14698               	; 	' sitting on, which is what made the messages hard to read. P1 is the HUD's
14699               	; 	' palette, dark blue and gold, so pointing the box's attribute bytes at it
14700               	; 	' gives a message the same treatment as the score line.
14701               	; 	'
14702               	; 	' FOUR BYTES AND NOT ONE MORE. An attribute byte covers four characters by
14703               	; 	' four, and the box is sized and placed to cover exactly four of them
14704               	; 	' (gentitle.py BOX_ROW/BOX_COL/BOX_W): byte columns 2..5, which is name
14705               	; 	' columns 8..23. Anything wider would recolour shop floor beside the box.
14706               	; 	'
14707               	; 	' THIS IS A ROUTINE BECAUSE IT WAS WRITTEN OUT TWICE AND MISSED A THIRD
14708               	; 	' TIME. GOT HIM! kept the store's colours while the other boxes changed,
14709               	; 	' and nothing failed -- it is a readable message in the wrong palette.
14710               	; 	' checkmsg.py now fails the build if a message box is drawn without one of
14711               	; 	' these beside it.
14712               	; 	'
14713               	; 	' Nothing puts them back, because nothing needs to: every path out of a
14714               	; 	' message box redraws the screen, and draw_screen calls nes_attr, which
14715               	; 	' rewrites all sixty-four.
14716               	; nes_boxatt:
14717               	; 	WAIT
14718               	; 	' Top half: P1 text. Bottom half: P3, whose navy matches P1 paper.
14719               	; 	' Only the third row is painted navy; leave the fourth row's tiles alone.

14826               	; 	' more like it -- four compares, four assignments and four jumps to walk a

14831               	; 	' when it changes and the clock once a second, so the cost is a handful of
14832               	; 	' DIVs a second against roughly sixty bytes of the one budget that is full.

15216               	;
15217               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
15218               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
15219               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
15220               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
15221               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
15222               	; 	'
15223               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
15224               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
15225               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
15226               	; 	'
15227               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
15228               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
15229               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
15230               	; 	'
15231               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
15232               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
15233               	; 	'
15234               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
15235               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
15236               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
15237               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
15238               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
15239               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
15240               	; 	'
15241               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
15242               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
15243               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
15244               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
15245               	; 	'
15246               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
15247               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
15248               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in
15249               	; 	' exchange for a truncation trap the next time somebody edits a band.)

15393               	;
15394               	; 	' AND IT ENDS ON ITS LAST BLIP -- there is no closing accent.
15395               	; 	'
15396               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
15397               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
15398               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
15399               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
15400               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
15401               	; 	'
15402               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
15403               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
15404               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
15405               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
15406               	; 	' counting stops.
15407               	;
15408               	; 	' `calc_bonus` USED TO LIVE HERE and computed the whole sum by repeated
15409               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
15410               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
15411               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
15412               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
15413               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
15414               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
15415               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.
15416               	; 	'
15417               	; 	' It also fixed the last-tick case for free: `bn_loop` tests `tsec = 0`
15418               	; 	' on entry, where the old `FOR bi = 1 TO tsec` would have run its body
15419               	; 	' once and paid a full multiplier for no time at all (CLAUDE.md 3A).
15420               	;

15463 F13E EF54     	data cvb_TIME_SHOW
15464               	; 	' THE CAST IS NOT TAKEN AWAY YET -- hide_all now runs AFTER the beat.
15465               	; 	'
15466               	; 	' It used to run here, so the moment the clock emptied, Harry and the
15467               	; 	' thing that had just hit him vanished and the sound played over an empty
15468               	; 	' store. The hit that ENDS a round is the worst case: `do_hit` sets tout
15469               	; 	' before the freeze starts and the main loop leaves on the very next pass,
15470               	; 	' so the hit sound gets one tick and everything is already gone.
15471               	; 	'
15472               	; 	' The pause drains the sound; leaving the actors up means it drains over
15473               	; 	' the picture that caused it. Nothing is moving -- the pause ticks sfx_tick
15474               	; 	' and nothing else -- so it is a held tableau, not a frozen game.
15475               	; 	' THE MESSAGE BOX, ON THE GAME SCREEN AND NOT INSTEAD OF IT.
15476               	; 	'
15477               	; 	' It used to CLS before GAME OVER, so the last thing the player saw was
15478               	; 	' the store being deleted and then two words on an empty field -- which
15479               	; 	' reads as the program ending rather than as the game ending. The store
15480               	; 	' stays; the message sits in the middle of it.
15481               	; 	'
15482               	; 	' THE BOX IS THE FONT'S OWN BACKGROUND. Every font character is black on
15483               	; 	' HUD_BG (dark blue), so a row of SPACES is a solid dark blue bar. A blank
15484               	; 	' row above and below the text is a frame for the price of two strings and
15485               	; 	' no new characters, and it reads against the store because nothing else on
15486               	; 	' the playfield is that colour.
15487               	; 	'
15488               	; 	' THIRTEEN WIDE, WHICH IS THE LONGEST MESSAGE PLUS ONE EITHER SIDE.
15489               	; 	' HE GOT AWAY and THE BIPLANE are both eleven. Every string below is padded
15490               	; 	' to exactly thirteen so the box has straight edges, and column 10 puts it
15491               	; 	' at columns 10-22 -- centre 16, the screen's.
15492               	; 	'
15493               	; 	' THE REASON IS ALWAYS ON THE SAME ROW, and that is what lets one layout
15494               	; 	' serve both cases. Losing a life draws three rows around it; losing the

15765               	;
15766               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
15767               	; 	'
15768               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
15769               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
15770               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
15771               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
15772               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
15773               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
15774               	; 	'
15775               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
15776               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
15777               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
15778               	; 	'
15779               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
15780               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
15781               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
15782               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
15783               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
15784               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
15785               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
15786               	; 	'
15787               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
15788               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
15789               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
15790               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
15791               	; 	'
15792               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
15793               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
15794               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
15795               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
15796               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
15797               	; 	'
15798               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
15799               	; 	' did not finish.
15800               	; pause_beat:

15850               	; 	' `SOUND ch,f,0` the last tone sustains for ever. And the second argument
15851               	; 	' is a 10-BIT DIVISOR, max 1023: SMALLER IS HIGHER, so a rising sweep is

16236               	; 	' player most needs to hear the hazards, and it fought the prize arpeggio
16237               	; 	' for channel 2 as well. The flash says the same thing and says it in the
16238               	; 	' place the player is already looking.
16239               	;
16240               	; 	' FOOTSTEPS ARE NOISE, AND ON THE NOISE CHANNEL -- testsounds variant A.
16241               	; 	'
16242               	; 	' They were two alternating TONES on channel 0, which is neither what the
16243               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
16244               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
16245               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
16246               	; 	'
16247               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
16248               	; 	'
16249               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
16250               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
16251               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
16252               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
16253               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
16254               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
16255               	; 	'
16256               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
16257               	; 	'
16258               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
16259               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
16260               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
16261               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
16262               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
16263               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
16264               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
16265               	; 	'
16266               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
16267               	; 	'
16268               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
16269               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
16270               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
16271               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
16272               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
16273               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
16274               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
16275               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
16276               	; 	'
16277               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
16278               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
16279               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
16280               	; 	'
16281               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
16282               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
16283               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
16284               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
16285               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
16286               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
16287               	; 	'
16288               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
16289               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.
16290               	; 	'
16291               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block
16292               	; 	' below runs LATER IN THE SAME sfx_tick, so a count of 1 is decremented to
16293               	; 	' zero on the pass that set it and the note-off fires before the sound has
16294               	; 	' lasted any time at all. 2 survives to the next pass, which is one pass of
16295               	; 	' sound -- about 42 ms against the bench's 33, as close as a per-pass timer
16296               	; 	' gets, and the reason the bench and the game cannot sound identical.
16297               	; 	'
16298               	; 	' Register 4 is white noise at the fastest rate.
16299               	; 	'
16300               	; 	' VOLUME 9, WHICH IS UNDER EVERYTHING ELSE ON PURPOSE. The hit, the prize
16301               	; 	' and the jump are 12 and 13, and they happen ONCE; footsteps play for the
16302               	; 	' whole round. At 13 they were level with the events they are supposed to
16303               	; 	' sit beneath, so the effects that carry information had nothing to stand
16304               	; 	' out from. The tone version was 7 for the same reason -- noise does read
16305               	; 	' quieter than a tone at the same number, which is why this is 9 and not
16306               	; 	' back to 7.

16604 F750 0450  20 	b *r0
16605               	;
16606               	; 	' A catch must not erase a life awarded on the same gameplay pass.
16607               	; life_finish:
16608               cvb_LIFE_FINISH
16609               	; 	GOSUB life_tick
16610 F752 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     F754 A980     
16611 F756 F66E     	data cvb_LIFE_TICK
16612               	; 	IF spt = 0 THEN RETURN
16613 F758 D020  34 	movb @cvb_SPT,r0
     F75A 222E     
16614 F75C 1602  14 	jne cv1040 ; shortened jeq / b
16615               	; removed long branch (shortbranches.py)
16616               cv1041
16617 F75E C03A  30 	mov *r10+,r0

16619               cv1040

16621 F762 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     F764 A980

16624 F768 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     F76A A980

16626               	; 	WAIT
16627 F76E 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     F770 A980     
16628 F772 A656     	data wait
16629               	; 	GOTO life_finish
16630 F774 0460  28 	b @cvb_LIFE_FINISH
     F776 F752     
16631               	;
16632               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1, so the INCLUDE order
16633               	; 	' is load-bearing and nothing but data may follow it.
16634               	; 	'
16635               	; 	' THE FONT IS NOW IN THE BANK TOO, and it used to be deliberately outside:
16636               	; 	' keeping one readable thing in bank 0 means a bank-selection mistake shows
16637               	; 	' as "text survives, art does not" rather than a uniformly blank screen,
16638               	; 	' which is a genuinely useful thing to have when a bank goes wrong.
16639               	; 	'
16640               	; 	' THE FONT HAS A BANK OF ITS OWN, and the reason is not its size.
16641               	; 	'
16642               	; 	' Bank 1 was FULL -- six spare bytes of 8,192 -- which shut the door on
16643               	; 	' moving anything else out of the fixed area, and the fixed area is the
16644               	; 	' only budget that cannot be grown (linkticart writes exactly three
16645               	; 	' loader pages and discards the rest; they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
16646               	; 	' >A000, not cart ROM). A second bank costs a bigger cart -- five pages
16647               	; 	' round up to eight, so 32 KB becomes 64 KB -- and buys back the ability
16648               	; 	' to keep evacuating data out of code.
16649               	; 	'
16650               	; 	' THE FONT IS THE RIGHT TENANT because it is read ONCE. Two DEFINEs copy
16651               	; 	' it into VRAM at setup and nothing looks at it again, so it is the only
16652               	; 	' block here that can sit on a page which is not permanently mapped. See
16653               	; 	' setup_font: bank 2 is selected for those two statements and bank 1 for
16654               	; 	' the whole of the rest of the program.
16655               	; 	'
16656               	; 	' EVERYTHING ELSE STAYS IN BANK 1, because everything else is read during
16657               	; 	' play -- art on a screen crossing, templates on a band blit, the lookup
16658               	; 	' tables every pass. One permanently-mapped bank for all of it means
16659               	; 	' there is no switch to miss.
16660               	; 	#if TI994A
16661               	; 	BANK 2
16662      0886     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$
     **** ****     > .rept

16801               	; 	' THE COLOUR TABLE, 472 bytes of the same value ($B4 = light yellow ink on dark blue).
16802               	; 	'
16803               	; 	' Loaded with DEFINE COLOR 32,59,font_col, which is ONE synchronous call that
16804               	; 	' writes all three screen thirds (define_color always does the LDIRVM3 triple
16805               	; 	' copy). It replaced a VPOKE loop that wrote this one value 1,416 times paced by
16806               	; 	' 24 WAITs -- the largest scripted delay in the boot, and the reason the title
16807               	; 	' screen used to fill in visibly rather than appearing at once.
16808               	; 	'
16809               	; 	' EIGHT BYTES PER CHARACTER, not one. Supply fewer and DEFINE COLOR reads
16810               	; 	' whatever follows in ROM as colour data, with no error at build or run time.
16811               	;

16934               	; 	' THE TITLE'S NAME -- whole kerned words, sliced

16936               	; 	' Do not edit here; edit the glyphs and rebuild.

16939               	; 	' repeated cells share a code. setup_font must load them
16940               	; 	' with EXACTLY these arguments:
16941               	; 	'     DEFINE CHAR    0,32,tfont_pat0
16942               	; 	'     DEFINE COLOR   0,32,tfont_col0
16943               	; 	'     DEFINE CHAR  185,12,tfont_pat1
16944               	; 	'     DEFINE COLOR 185,12,tfont_col1
16945               	; 	'
16946               	; 	' LIVES IN BANK 2 -- read once by those DEFINEs.
16947               	; 	' ==================================================

17476               	; 	INCLUDE "art.bas"
17477               	; 	' Keystone Kapers art -- GENERATED by assets/genart.py. Do not edit; regenerate.
17478               	; 	'
17479               	; 	' EVERY SPRITE IS 16x16: sprite size and magnification are GLOBAL on the
17480               	; 	' TMS9918, so small objects are drawn small INSIDE a 16x16 box rather than
17481               	; 	' being small sprites.
17482               	; 	'
17483               	; 	' EVERY 8-PX OBJECT SITS IN ROWS 8-15 OF ITS BOX, ducked Kelly included, so
17484               	; 	' one rule places them all: bottom edge = y + 16, and a thing resting on the
17485               	; 	' floor is at y = FLOORY - 16.
17486               	; 	'
17487               	; 	' Sprite bytes are QUADRANT-ORDERED: 16 rows of the left half, then 16 of
17488               	; 	' the right. Every block is an EVEN number of bytes -- an odd DATA BYTE run
17489               	; 	' silently misaligns every word table after it (CLAUDE.md 3A).
17490               	;
17491               	; spr_kelly:	' Kelly: RIGHT hat/face/two merged run bodies/two FREE slots/duck hat/face/body, then the same LEFT (+36). The run bodies carry tunic AND legs, so a frame is one sprite, and standing is run frame 1. Patterns 0..68

18723               	; 	INCLUDE "store.bas"
18724               	; 	' Keystone Kapers store -- GENERATED by assets/genstore.py. Do not edit.
18725               	; 	'
18726               	; 	' EIGHT band templates of 5 rows x 32 cols (160 bytes each) plus a 32-byte
18727               	; 	' index over (level, screen). The whole 8-screen, 4-level building is about
18728               	; 	' 1.3 KB instead of the 5,120 bytes it would cost to store literally.
18729               	; 	'
18730               	; 	' All eight templates are ONE contiguous block under ONE label, so a band
18731               	; 	' blit is
18732               	; 	'     SCREEN stor_tpl, tpl*160, toprow*32, 32, 5, 32
18733               	; 	' with no label ladder -- SCREEN needs a literal label and a label cannot be
18734               	; 	' chosen by a variable, which is why RallyX needed a 4-way IF over its maze
18735               	; 	' tables. One block sidesteps it.
18736               	; 	'
18737               	; 	' 160 is EVEN, so this cannot leave the location counter odd and misalign
18738               	; 	' the word tables defined after it.
18739               	; 	'
18740               	; 	' template ids:
18741               	; 	'   0 T_AISLE_A
18742               	; 	'   1 T_AISLE_B
18743               	; 	'   2 T_ESC_W
18744               	; 	'   3 T_ESC_E
18745               	; 	'   4 T_ELEV
18746               	; 	'   5 T_ROOF0
18747               	; 	'   6 T_ROOF1
18748               	; 	'   7 T_ROOF2
18749               	; 	'   8 T_ROOF3
18750               	; 	'   9 T_ROOF4
18751               	; 	'   10 T_ROOF5
18752               	; 	'   11 T_ROOF6
18753               	; 	'   12 T_ROOF7
18754               	; 	'   13 T_END_W
18755               	; 	'   14 T_END_E
18756               	;
18757               	; stor_tpl:	' 15 templates x 160 bytes
18758               cvb_STOR_TPL

19373               	;
19374               	; 	' THE SKYLINE'S LAST BAND WITHOUT ITS YELLOW, high nibble ink, low nibble
19375               	; 	' paper, one byte a scan line -- the same shape genart emits into
19376               	; 	' store_col. SKY2 is white-on-9 throughout instead of turning to paper 10
19377               	; 	' at row 4; BLDGL holds its blue one row longer and then meets its own
19378               	; 	' grey wall. Both are the generated bytes with 10 replaced by 9 and
19379               	; 	' nothing else changed. See setup_rest.
19380               	; #if NES
19381               	; nes_sky2c:
19382               	; 	DATA BYTE $F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9
19383               	; nes_bldlc:
19384               	; 	DATA BYTE $B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$BE,$BE,$BE
19385               	; #endif
19386               	;
19387               	; 	' THE IN-GAME FONT'S COLOUR, one byte a scan line and eight a character for
19388               	; 	' all 59 of them. $B4 is light yellow on dark blue -- ink index 3, paper index 1 --
19389               	; 	' and which colours those are is then the attribute table's business, per
19390               	; 	' region: dark blue behind the HUD, the store's green behind a message box.
19391               	; 	'
19392               	; 	' 472 bytes of one repeated value. That reads like waste and is the cheap
19393               	; 	' option: ROM is three budgets here and this is not the scarce one, while
19394               	; 	' the alternative is a second font (impossible -- only eleven free codes)
19395               	; 	' or a new uploader parameter (no RAM -- two bytes left).

19397               	; nes_fcol:
